title: Enumerations and typedef
description: Named integer constants with enum, and creating type aliases with typedef.
objectives: Define and use enums for named integer constants
Combine typedef with struct/enum for cleaner syntax

content.heading: enum: Named Integer Constants
content.body: enum Color { RED, GREEN, BLUE }; declares a set of named integer constants — by default, RED is 0, GREEN is 1, BLUE is 2, sequentially assigned unless overridden explicitly (enum Color { RED = 1, GREEN, BLUE }; makes GREEN 2 and BLUE 3, continuing sequentially from an explicit value). enum Color favoriteColor = GREEN; declares a variable of that enum type. Under the hood, an enum in C is really just an int with named values for readability — the compiler does not strictly enforce that a Color variable only ever holds RED/GREEN/BLUE; comparing it to an arbitrary unrelated integer is legal (if semantically meaningless) C, unlike Java's considerably more type-safe enums.

content.heading: typedef
content.body: typedef creates an alias for an existing type: typedef unsigned long ulong; lets ulong be used anywhere unsigned long could be, purely for readability/brevity. typedef is especially common paired with struct and enum, since referring to a plain struct type in C otherwise always requires repeating the struct keyword: typedef struct { int x, y; } Point; lets you write Point p; instead of the more verbose struct Point p; every time (note this particular form defines an anonymous struct with the typedef name attached directly, a very common idiom). typedef is purely a compile-time convenience — it introduces no new type at runtime, only an alternate name the compiler treats identically to the original type.

content.explanation: ACTIVE prints as 1, confirming enum constants are just named integers under the hood. Point and Priority demonstrate typedef eliminating the need to repeat struct/enum at every variable declaration.

keyPoints: enum defines named integer constants, sequentially numbered from 0 unless overridden
C enums are weakly type-checked — they're really just named ints, unlike Java's stronger enum type safety
typedef creates a compile-time-only alias for an existing type, introducing no new runtime type
typedef struct {...} Name; is the common idiom for using a struct type without repeating the struct keyword
commonMistakes: Assuming C enums prevent assigning an arbitrary, unrelated integer value (they don't enforce this)
Forgetting the struct keyword when declaring a struct variable without a typedef alias in place
Assuming typedef creates a genuinely distinct type rather than just an alternate name for an existing one
